rewrites.blindSummary: This country is workable for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct was decriminalised in 2016; the constitution guarantees equal protection; and the country is a small, tourism-dependent state/province with extremely low violent crime and long exposure to international visitors. There is no legal gender recognition and no documented trans-specific infrastructure, but also no documented pattern of anti-trans violence or police hostility.
rewrites.blindTangential: The 2016 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Legal gender recognition absence is resident-facing; evidence is thin given the tiny population.
blindSourceSummaries: Legal-information institute's gender-justice page on this country: under the penal code amendment act 2024 (Act 13 of 2024) section 5, protected characteristics now include sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics and HIV/AIDS status, giving an enhanced-protection basis for hate-motivated offences; the constitution separately guarantees freedom from torture (Article 16) and equal protection with non-discrimination on grounds including sex (Article 27).

News outlet report, 18 May 2016: this country repealed a historic-era penal-code provision (Section 151) which had allowed up to 14 years' imprisonment for male same-sex sex, framed as the popular holiday destination opening its arms to LGBT people.

Travel guide: notes the 2016 decriminalisation of same-sex acts as a significant victory for the country, while advising both local residents and tourists to stay vigilant and informed about the current legal and social landscape — practical visitor guidance for the destination.

Rights-media outlet, 27 September 2024: a newly revised law calls for increased prison sentences for violent crimes motivated by hostility toward victims' sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics, race, religion or disability — per a human-rights legal organisation, this country is one of only two countries to protect against all forms of hate-based victimisation; before 2016 the penal code punished male same-sex intimacy with up to 14 years.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is dangerous for trans visitors. The 2006 criminal law act criminalises sodomy (up to 1 year — a lighter formal penalty than in comparable countries, though indecency provisions add exposure), and an international rights organisation's 2024 report documents shrinking civic space threatening LGBT organising (the main local LGBT organisation operates under pressure; its offices have been raided historically). There is no legal gender recognition, political rhetoric is hostile, and mob violence is documented — but prosecution under the sodomy law is rarer than in comparable countries, and a small organised community persists openly enough to litigate.

For a visitor: statutory exposure exists but enforcement is sporadic; social hostility is the main risk.
rewrites.blindTangential: Sodomy criminalised (up to 1 year, sporadic enforcement) — formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Same-sex criminalisation is the vehicle; enforcement pattern is sporadic.
blindSourceSummaries: Human-rights legal organisation's country profile: this country criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women (sodomy and 'acts involving contact between males that would be regarded by a reasonable person as indecent'); only the opening of the profile was retrievable at fetch time.

International rights organisation report, 9 January 2024: documents escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment, the weaponisation of law and their human-rights implications in select countries; the cached copy is only the title/index page — it fixes the report's date, scope and thesis but contains no country-specific passages, so it cannot carry incident-level claims; treat it as the report's existence record, not its evidence.

News outlet report, 9 July 2018: the health ministry released a training handbook for all health practitioners on serving gays, sex workers and transgender/non-gender-conforming people in public health institutions; the manual states care for these groups is legal and every provider's duty, and was issued because patients had avoided clinics fearing mistreatment or police tip-offs by staff; for a trans visitor: formal policy guarantees health-service access including transition-relevant care at public facilities, though day-to-day treatment depends on staff trained under a 2018 handbook.

Academic article, 'The politics of sexual identities in this country: A social work perspective?' (International Journal of Humanities and Social Science, July 2012): homosexuals live secluded lives due to prejudice; the article traces same-sex relations in this country before and after historic administration; social workers should promote social justice for the gay community.
Academic publisher (Journal of Homosexuality): academic article on homosexuality in this country — the page consisted largely of navigation content at fetch time.

The main local LGBT organisation's official site: a long-standing voluntary membership organisation with thousands of community members, many years of advocacy and multiple affinity groups and resource centres; services include legal support (explicitly including for 'sodomy' arrests), counselling, hospital-fee assistance and empowerment programmes for local LGBTI people; for the record: documented local support infrastructure — legal aid and counselling reachable despite criminalisation, useful for an LGBTI traveller needing assistance.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Article 152 of the penal code criminalises gender nonconformity directly; sodomy carries life imprisonment (capital/corporal punishment removed in 2020 reforms); and a rights documentation project documents official violence against LGBTQIA+ people including extrajudicial killings. Since April 2023 the country has been in a catastrophic civil war between two armed factions with documented mass atrocities — the conflict intensifies every risk and eliminates any recourse. There is no legal gender recognition and no community infrastructure.

For a visitor: statutory criminalisation of gender nonconformity plus one of the world's worst active conflicts.
rewrites.blindTangential: Sodomy carries life imprisonment — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: War conditions affect all; Article 152 is trans-specific.
blindSourceSummaries: A rights documentation project's profile of this country: penal code Article 152 criminalises wearing clothing of the opposite sex (cross-dressing provisions); no arrest statistics for trans people but documented official violence including extrajudicial killings against LGBTQIA+ individuals; no legal gender recognition; gender-affirming healthcare legally constrained; the ongoing conflict further restricts access; and official reliance on religious edicts blocks transition. Gender-nonconformity framing for visitor risk.

A human-rights legal organisation's country profile: this country criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, with sentences including a maximum of life imprisonment (and historically the death penalty for a third offence); only the opening was retrievable at fetch time.

A foreign government's 2010 human-rights report on this country: documents the then-ruling regime's abuses — extrajudicial killings, torture, an armed conflict — and the LGBT section noting criminalisation under Article 148 with flogging and death-penalty provisions.

Academic authors (2014), 'Homosexuality in this country and a neighbouring country: Stories of the Struggle for Survival' — by a university research fellow with activists of the regional LGBTQI organisation; explores daily struggles, discrimination and violence rooted in societal gender and sexual norms, and whether post-uprising change will transform circumstances.

A community magazine of this country: runs sections on LGBTI rights in this country (history and analysis) and a profile of the country and its LGBTI organisations, i.e. documents an organised local community presence; landing/index page: thin for current findings.

Rights-media outlet (15 July 2020): this country's governing council removed the death penalty for homosexuality — maximum now life imprisonment for a third offence — abolished the 100 lashes for same-sex intimacy, and set up to five years' imprisonment for a first offence in the criminal-code amendment.

rewrites.blindSummary:

For a visitor: statutory risk plus a near-total absence of protective institutions.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — one of the world's most dangerous countries for any LGBT person. The penal code criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 3 years), but the operative reality is worse: a militant group controls significant areas and applies its interpretation of religious law, under which homosexuality and gender transgression are capital offences — executions are documented. Even in government areas, mob violence and clan-justice dynamics make any gender nonconformity lethal-risk. There is no legal gender recognition, no community, and no recourse of any kind.

For a visitor: there is no safe way to be visibly trans anywhere in the country.
rewrites.blindTangential: Same-sex conduct criminalised (up to 3 years) and capital under the militant group's religious law — a catastrophic exposure for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Fragmented authority means enforcement varies; areas under militant-group control apply capital punishment.
blindSourceSummaries: Source note: not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying human-rights legal organisation's country profile documents this country's criminalisation of same-sex sexual activity (up to life imprisonment under the 1964 penal code; death penalty under religious law in some regions).

A foreign government's 2021 human-rights report on this country: official assessment — same-sex conduct criminalised (up to 3 years); a militant group enforces strict religious law with death as possible punishment; pervasive violence and statelessness.

A foreign government's 2022 human-rights report on this country: criminalises 'carnal intercourse with a person of the same sex', 3 months' to 3 years' imprisonment, no official reports of enforcement available; under local interpretations of religious law, homosexuality is punishable by death; no known official executions of that sort reported; impunity generally remained the norm.

A foreign government's 2010 human-rights report on this country (archived): documents the conflict, abuses by a militant group, and the LGBT section noting criminalisation and the death penalty under religious law in areas under insurgent control.

Rights-media outlet (16 February 2016) on a researcher's 'Report on the Treatment of Gay Persons in this country' (published 2 February 2016): evidence that gay persons should not be returned to this country due to persecution risk, supporting refugee-status claims; notes the country's anti-homosexuality law provides up to ... [report excerpt] — non-refoulement basis for LGBT asylum seekers.

International news outlet (July 2013), 'Gay refugees from this country face death threats': refugees in a neighbouring country face threats and racist discrimination, with a militant group publicising intent to enforce harsh punishments against homosexuality and senior figures claiming gay people would face death if returned; UN officials nevertheless pushed return — dated account of persecution driving displacement.

rewrites.blindSummary: This country is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Article 310(1) of the 2015 penal code criminalises 'homosexual conduct' (up to 7 years), there are no anti-discrimination protections of any kind, and this country is among the world's most closed societies — indefinite national service, mass arbitrary detention, no independent media, no civil society, and no way to document conditions. The country has rejected every sexual-orientation-and-gender-identity recommendation at every universal-periodic-review cycle. Nothing is known about trans people in this country because nothing can be known — the absence of data reflects total informational control.
rewrites.blindTangential: Article 310(1) criminalises homosexual conduct (up to 7 years) — trans visitors are captured via birth-sex status.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Documentation absence reflects totalitarian informational control.
blindSourceSummaries: International LGBTI-rights organisation country overview (updated 12 March 2026): Article 310(1) of the penal code criminalises 'homosexual conduct' with up to 7 years' imprisonment — inherited from the 1957 penal code of the parent nation and retained with an enhanced sentence in the first post-independence penal code (adopted 2015).

A foreign government's 2023 human-rights report on this country: section 7 records that openly LGBTQI+ persons risked imprisonment and therefore did not participate in the political process; societal discrimination against LGBTQI+ persons continues alongside a law making no gender distinction for assault.

A foreign government's 2010 human-rights report on this country (archived): documents the authoritarian regime's abuses — torture, arbitrary detention, indefinite national service — with the LGBT section noting criminalisation and societal stigma.

News relay of a foreign government's 2011 human-rights report on this country: societal abuse and discrimination against gay men and lesbians occurred; the government labelled disloyal individuals with anti-gay and other abusive epithets; the law criminalises consensual same-sex sexual activity.

A foreign government's 'country of concern' human-rights report (2015): same-sex activity is a crime in this country and there is no anti-discrimination legislation protecting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people; the reporting government raised these concerns bilaterally and via a regional bloc.
